questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Choosing a culture i didnt know in a place that is less touristy.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Super fun experience that i would recommend everyone!

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: They send you information beforehand thats pretty comprehensive. After arrival at the dormitory (thats the first destination) they will kind of hold your hand through the rest of the process.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: They help you out the first day with getting settled at the dormitory. Afterwards there are a lot of introductory orientations the first 2 weeks

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Ohmeikan and Daiko are the main 2 options. Both are cheap (20000 and 30000 yen per month, respectively). Ohmeikan is 10 min walk from campus, while Daiko is 10 minute subway away.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: There was a kitchen in the dormitory for cooking. Otherwise restaurants are incredibly cheap here, so you can eat out a lot without worrying too much.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Ohmeikan is cheap and close but extremely dirty. I often wouldnt cook my own food since the kitchen was that bad. Also, there are a lot of rules when living there. No eating or drinking in the huge common are/lobby, alcohol completely forbidden(except for drinking on your own in your room apparently), and no noise allowed after 12. Also, parties are prohibited and boys cant go to the girls floor. Its more of a place to sleep than a place where you will do activities.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Only reason it's a 3 is because of the location and the price, which in the end is the most important. Just know that its pretty damn dirty and messy.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
You find the courses you want on the syllabi, write down the codes, and submit them to a website given to you in the orientations. You are also allocated an academic advisor that just has to sign your choice of courses. Afterwards its done! I had a hard time finding a syllabi that felt up to date, so below  are attached 2 links to the syllabi from my autumn semester. First link is for NUPACE courses (culture related and languages), and the second is for the G30 program courses (Courses in your major taught in english, taken together with the G30 students who are doing their whole degree at NU)
NUPACE:
https://nuss.nagoya-u.ac.jp/s/5Twsmno24Y64wBx
G30:
https://nuss.nagoya-u.ac.jp/s/gWXjmWkwNks824o

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Nupace office are always available, and the huge amount of orientations should cover all you'd need.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Got all the courses i wanted!

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Take a japanese class if you can. I didnt because i was unsure if i would get the credits transferred if i did. But if you can check that beforehand, i'd highly recommend it. Seemed very useful and fun.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: 8/9 of my courses were G30. G30 is very competitive to get enrolled in, so expect the courses to be hard. I'd say every course thats worth 2 credits (4ects) are equivalent to maybe 6-7.5 ECTS.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: NUPACE courses and language courses are supposedly super easy and not challenging at all. The G30 courses on the other hand are notoriously hard. Be prepared! Its not just a vacation, you got to put in actual work.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: UCPH is much more in depth and theoretical than NU. Here it is more about covering as big a curriculum as possible by only scraping the surface, and talking about how it can be applied. I by far prefer UCPH but to each their own. Also know that, if you're doing courses in science, you will have to use things from the curriculum (like specific equations) in the exam that you will not have used beforehand in assignments and tutorials.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Biochemistry I
Particle physics
Condensed matter physics I
Physics tutorial 1a (tutorial for analytical mechanics)
Chemical physics
Intercultural competence
Physical chemistry I
Analytical mechanics I
Earth and planetary sciences

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Analytical mechanics I is super good if you havent done it at KU. Physical chemistry is also super interesting in how it applied thermodynamics to more specific chemical systems. Chemical physics is more of a hardcore indepth look on thermodynamics which i enjoyed a lot

But most of all, do a japanese course if you can! It's 5 credits (10 ECTS) and super useful. I regret not doing it due to missing out on so much fun with the other exchange students.

If you are a physics student, i would personally strongly advice against doing classes with John Wojdylo. While he is a nice guy, his 2 credit courses would be the equivalent to 15 ECTS in workload, it is absolutely ludicrous. So only do them if you're ready to study for his class every single day of the week for multiple hours.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: They dont use books here for courses, so that cost is out of the way.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food and rent is dirt cheap here, so dont worry too much about a scholarship; its easily manageable without one. Public transport is the same price as in Copenhagen, so be warned. Otherwise japan is super cheap!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Lots of clubs to join, and a lot of advertisements for them in the first couple of weeks upon arrival!

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Sports clubs were everywhere, especially Judo club was popular (they pay for the dinner afterwards). Lots of advertisements all the time for cultural activities and such, so you wont miss out.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go traveling! Super beautiful country that is not worth missing out on.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go traveling the countryside! I'm not a big fan of Kyoto, Osaka and Tokyo due to the overtourism. So going to some random place is amazing. I'd recommend Noto peninsula and Kyuushuu!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Just be polite and try not to be loud. The japanese people are very reserved and introverted by nature, so try and respect their boundaries.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Learn japanese, preferably get to N3 level if you want to actually have japanese friends. The japanese people know next to no english, so if you want to socialize with them its kind of a must. Also enroll in the tutoring system! The tutors are somewhat proficient in english and can be a gateway to meeting other japanese.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Everything is paid in cash. be prepared to pay your rent physically using cash at the convenience store every month.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: How nice the japanese are! Especially if you try and speak japanese to them, they appreciate it a lot.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Nagoya is a wonderful city that you'd probably never heard of. I chose it for that exact reason. Going here in contrast to tokyo or kyoto will give you a much more authenic experience of what living japan is really like. You'll feel like a local and not a tourist

Nagoya uni campus is very pleasant and centralized, so theres not that far between your classes. And the G30 students are super nice, try and socialize with them

Nagoya is also placed in the middle of Japan, making weekend trips and travels so much more manageable. Cant recommend it enough

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Plugin-lab is this place underneath the northern canteen where you can study and get FREE coffee, tea, cocoa, Soda and more! I spent like 80% of my week days there.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting people from other nationalities, not just the japanese. Everyones kind of on their own, so its like you're setting your life at home on a pause and starting a new one here with the other exchange students!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Language. Learn it beforehand if you can. And if you cant, try and enroll in the japanese classes.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Have fun here! Nagoya is a wonderful city with wonderful people.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
